title: Trying to keep both
literal_meaning: The friend will remain; the jewel will remain.
explanation: The words sound reassuring: neither precious thing need be lost. But the dictionary labels the saying ironic and applies it to someone who tries to preserve both sides and succeeds with neither. The sting lies in that gap between a comfortable promise and what actually happens. It can tease an attempt to avoid a difficult choice, rather than praise a successful compromise.
meaning_odia: ମିତ ବି ରହିବ, ମାଣିକ ବି ରହିବ—ଶୁଣିଲେ ଲାଗେ କିଛି ହରାଇବାକୁ ପଡ଼ିବ ନାହିଁ। ହେଲେ ଅଭିଧାନର ବ୍ୟଙ୍ଗ ଅର୍ଥରେ ଦୁଇ ପଟକୁ ରଖିବାକୁ ଯାଇ ଶେଷରେ କୌଣସି ପଟକୁ ରଖି ହୁଏ ନାହିଁ। ସବୁ ଠିକ୍ ରହିବ ବୋଲି କହିବା ଓ ପ୍ରକୃତରେ ସମ୍ଭାଳିବା ଭିତରର ଫରକଟି ଏଠି ଧରାପଡ଼େ। କଠିନ ନିଷ୍ପତ୍ତିକୁ ଏଡ଼ାଇବାର ଚେଷ୍ଟା ଦେଖି କେହି ଏହାକୁ ଟିକେ ଟାହି କରି କହିପାରନ୍ତି।
english_summary: An ironic promise to preserve both sides ends with neither secured.
odia_summary: ଦୁଇ ପଟ ରଖିବାର ଆଶ୍ୱାସନ ଶେଷରେ ଦୁଇ ପଟ ହରାଇବାର ବ୍ୟଙ୍ଗ ହୁଏ।
usage_example: A person promises to attend two gatherings at the same time, keeps postponing a decision and misses both; a friend uses the saying. (Original imagined example, not collected testimony.)
cultural_context: The ironic, unsuccessful outcome follows the explicit dictionary gloss, not an inferred win-win moral. Friend/jewel are a literal reading, not identified historical characters or objects. Source-listed parallels are not claimed as independently verified variants.
